title: Bibliometric Analysis of the Korean Journal of Parasitology: Measured from SCI, PubMed, Scopus, and Synapse Databases
extended_summary:
This paper is not the requested secondary study on ChatGPT and senior high school students' academic writing. Instead, it is a bibliometric analysis of the Korean Journal of Parasitology (KJP) conducted for the 50th anniversary of the Korean Society for Parasitology. The study asks how much scholarly impact the journal has had over its publication history and compares citation counts and related metrics across four databases: SCI/Web of Science, PubMed/PMC, Scopus, and Synapse/CrossRef.

The approach is a database-based citation analysis rather than an educational intervention study. The author collected citation records for 1,370 KJP articles published from 1963 to August 2009 and examined numbers of cited articles, total citations, average citations, highly cited papers, impact factors, and h-index values. A major analytic focus is on how database coverage, title changes, DOI assignment, and self-citations affect bibliometric indicators.

There are no student, teacher, or school participants. The context is scholarly publishing and citation indexing, with the journal based in Korea and the analysis conducted using international bibliographic databases. The paper discusses how Synapse/CrossRef captured many citations to older articles that were missed or undercounted in other databases, especially those published under the journal's earlier Korean title.

The main conclusion is that KJP has made sustained and internationally visible contributions to parasitology, with over 60% of its articles cited at least once in SCI and even higher coverage in Synapse. The paper argues that DOI-based linking and broader indexing improve journal visibility and citation capture, and that KJP's impact is likely to continue increasing after its inclusion in SCI.
